approach.method_basis: The Parent samples local graph edits from one scored molecule, sanitizes and normalizes each result, rejects prior identities and directly evaluates a full batch allowed by inverse-motif memory. It selects the best accepted neighbor even when that move lowers score and separately retains its best archive. Its atom and attachment menus are governed by graph valence and available hydrogens, so a halogen can attach directly to nitrogen, oxygen or sulfur as well as carbon. The repaired identity join and the established memory lifecycle are part of this Parent.
approach.novelty: Add one source-relative attachment gate: a new neighbor may not increase the number of halogen bonds to non-carbon heavy atoms. Carbon-bound halogens remain eligible under the existing rules. The gate changes which fresh neighbors proceed to tabu testing and evaluation while keeping every edit draw unchanged. The earlier sulfur filter targeted a sulfur valence envelope, and the positional experiments changed local molecular construction; this experiment isolates the remaining halogen attachment pattern and combines none of those mechanisms.

hypothesis: Reject a graph-valid canonically novel neighbor before tabu testing when it increases the source-relative count of bonds between F, Cl, Br or I and a non-carbon heavy atom, redirecting the existing edit stream away from new non-carbon halogen attachment while preserving carbon-halogen eligibility and the Parent walk.

finding_summary.headline: Non-carbon halogen attachments disappear, but the gate fails score non-inferiority
finding_summary.insights: The attachment criterion has a distinct effect beyond existing tabu memory: every measured rejection changes which fresh neighbor can reach evaluation. It also separates carbon-bound halogens from direct nitrogen-, oxygen- and sulfur-halogen bonds, rather than simply eliminating all halogen-containing molecules. The chemistry cleanup therefore happened, but its score cost is real in this panel. The Parent had obtained six immediate archive improvements from count-increasing moves, so this was never a uniformly unhelpful channel; those historical scores do not label the different rejected products. The rule is source-relative and would permit equal or lower counts on a molecule with pre-existing counted bonds. Its complete absence here depends on the zero-count starting states. Other liabilities remain outside the mechanism: the molecular assessment still finds unusual sulfur coordination, dense bridges, small unsaturated rings and undefined stereochemistry. Removing one attachment class neither establishes generally plausible chemistry nor preserves objective performance.
finding_summary.results: The gate rejected 130 valid, novel attachment increases; all 130 would otherwise pass the contemporaneous tabu rule, and each was followed by another actual neighbor from the same source. Starting from zero-count molecules, the complete panel emitted no targeted bonds, compared with 974 affected Parent emissions. Carbon-halogen chemistry remained active in 2670 evaluated molecules versus 2596 before, including 265 source improvements and 153 archive gains. Generation attempts per batch rose from 12.15 to 12.63. The macro mean fell from 0.520918 to 0.513044, a paired loss of 0.007874 exceeding the permitted 0.002. Gains in DRD2 and some other endpoints did not offset the larger sitagliptin losses.

molecular.headline: Tightly sized ring-rich molecules retain unusual sulfur centres, dense bridges and undefined stereochemistry
molecular.overall_character: The complete panel contains 900 evaluated molecules per task across three seeds, including 870 optimizer proposals each. All 4,350 optimizer proposals parse with RDKit. Every proposal contains a ring-closure digit, and digest aromatic-token rates range from 0.8667 to 1.0; rings are abundant. Proposal heavy-atom ranges are tightly concentrated at 21-29, 30-48, 29-43, 28-45 and 26-34 in fixed task order, with no proposal above 50 heavy atoms. Nevertheless, these are not uniformly simple molecules: median ring counts are three, four, four, five and six, and the last task reaches 17 perceived rings within its limited atom range. Recognizable ketones, thioesters, lactams, ethers, phenols and amines coexist with unusual sulfur coordination, highly fused or bridged graphs and small unsaturated rings. Proposals with explicit-H sulfur atoms bonded to at least two heavy atoms number 50, 138, 747, 192 and 554. These [SH] sites should not be read as ordinary terminal thiols. Direct N-halogen and O-halogen bonds are absent from current proposals, whereas they occurred in the parent, but unusual sulfur and ring chemistry remains pervasive. All proposals have zero charged-string markers; neutrality does not establish ordinary valence chemistry or stable solution species. Per-task nonchiral Murcko scaffold counts are 430, 418, 452, 442 and 521, while leaders remain concentrated in a few related families. No proposal assigns a stereocentre; 624, 396, 870, 668 and 780 contain unassigned centres. I read the dominant sulfur-rich high-score families as implausible practical synthetic targets without substantial chemical validation, while some ketone, thioester and lactam alternatives are more recognizable. The assessment concerns chemical appearance, not demonstrated synthesis or activity.

per_task.generated_character: The highest structure combines an unsaturated sulfur/nitrogen bicycle with a carboxamide and an N-acyl nitrogen closing a three-membered ring across adjacent aromatic carbons. It has 24 heavy atoms and four perceived rings, but only one aromatic ring. The next family is more recognizable: substituted indene-like ketones or heteroaryl thioesters, often with amino, alkoxy or bromoethyl groups. Several carry an O/N/S-substituted carbon connected to a bromomethyl group, a chemically different motif from a simple ether. Parent leaders included N-halogenated amide or sulfur-containing fused frameworks. Current direct N-halogen proposals fall from 172 to zero, but sulfur and ring-bond alterations persist. Full proposals have median 25 heavy atoms and three rings.
liabilities: The highest N-acyl substituent contains a three-membered ring fused to an aromatic bond, a substantial geometry concern despite successful parsing.
Bromomethyl or bromoethyl arms and O/N/S-substituted carbons introduce potential reactivity and stability questions.
Sulfur double-bond and coordination changes must be assessed in context; ordinary thioesters should not be equated with unusual cyclic sulfur centres.
missing_features: Stable, conventional alternatives preserving the useful fused-ring/carbonyl placement are underrepresented among leaders relative to sulfur-valence and ring-closure variants.
The leading three-membered N-ring and heteroatom-rich side-chain structures lack established geometry or synthetic access, and 624 proposals have unassigned centres.
per_task.score_gradient_reading: The sulfur/strained-N-ring structure scores 0.425403 and an indene-like heteroaryl thioester 0.424583, so the unusual first topology is not the only visible route to a similar value. A bromoethyl ether ketone scores 0.412377, while O/N/S-substituted analogues lie around 0.39-0.42. These examples associate a compact fused aromatic/carbonyl arrangement with appreciable score, without isolating a benefit from unusual sulfur or reactive side chains. Low optimizer proposals, approximately 0.008-0.035, already have many rings and polar groups but alter the connecting topology, aromatic region or cyclic carbonyl context. Terminal ring-contracted or heavily altered sulfur structures fall around 0.13-0.34. The overall score minimum includes initial molecules; the cited optimizer minimum is 0.008082.

per_task.generated_character: The leading family contains two substituted aromatic rings connected through a benzyl-bound neutral [SH] centre also bonded to nitrogen, with imine, urea-like and thiocarbonyl substituents. Many displayed variants retain almost the entire framework while changing carbonyl versus sulfur groups, alkyl length or terminal unsaturation. Relative to the parent, explicit-H sulfur with multiple heavy-atom neighbours increases from 46 to 138 proposals, while direct N-halogen bonds fall from 29 to zero. liabilities: A neutral sulfur atom bearing explicit hydrogen and several heavy-atom bonds is not an ordinary thiol; its stability cannot be inferred from neutral SMILES syntax.
Displayed leaders have molecular masses around 640-720 despite fewer than 50 heavy atoms, showing that atom-count moderation does not remove substantial mass burden.
Thiocarbonyl, imine and sulfur-rich side chains create unresolved reactivity and tautomeric issues in a largely repeated framework.
missing_features: The high-score neighborhood lacks demonstrated ordinary-linker alternatives preserving its aromatic and polar arrangement without a multiply connected [SH] centre.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Counts of proposals with explicit-H sulfur bonded to at least two heavy atoms are 50, 138, 747, 192 and 554 across the five sessions. Ordinary thioesters and other recognizable sulfur functional groups also occur and should be distinguished from the unusual centres.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator lacks reliable support for ordinary stable sulfur environments rather than merely graph-valid sulfur coordination.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Provide stable bonding and electronic environments that preserve useful observed polar relationships, with chemical distinctions among thioesters, thioethers, sulfonamides and unusual neutral sulfur centres. Neutral syntax and parser acceptance cannot serve as substitutes for credible molecular chemistry.

transferable_gaps.evidence: All proposal heavy-atom ranges remain between 21 and 48, with none above 50. Yet a leading 36-heavy-atom molecule has eight perceived rings and mass 604.676, while a 30-heavy-atom leader has six rings and another has ten. Medium and large N/O cycles also occur among leaders. The highest molecules in one session have masses around 640-720 despite only 39-42 heavy atoms.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator controls atom counts without consistently controlling feasible ring topology, mass or synthetic complexity.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Support chemically credible ring closures and lower-burden core alternatives within the observed size range. Atom count alone does not capture bridge strain, accessible conformations, elemental mass or synthetic difficulty; these properties need distinct representation in the generated chemistry.

transferable_gaps.evidence: No stereocentres are assigned in 4,350 optimizer proposals. The five sessions contain 624, 396, 870, 668 and 780 proposals with unassigned centres. Every proposal in one session is stereogenic by RDKit perception, and a displayed high-score 30-heavy-atom cage has eleven unassigned centres. Another highest molecule has six. Ring richness and saturated complexity therefore do not establish defined three-dimensional proposals.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator proposes complex stereogenic molecules without specifying any of their configurations.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Represent chemically consistent configurations and relevant bond geometries where they exist, retaining simpler achiral alternatives when appropriate. The supplied evidence does not choose an unobserved stereoisomer, and adding stereogenic ring junctions without specification does not provide interpretable molecular geometry.

transferable_gaps.evidence: Per-session nonchiral Murcko scaffold counts are 430, 418, 452, 442 and 521, but displayed leaders repeatedly occupy the same sulfur-linked aromatic, bridged amine or polycyclic carbonyl neighborhoods. Many carbonyl/sulfur/alkyl variants share score 0.608402, and several alkoxy or ring-atom alternatives share 0.207549. Low and high examples can both contain abundant sulfur or rings, showing that raw counts do not specify useful polar and aromatic relationships.
transferable_gaps.gap: The generator has limited chemically distinct productive alternatives beyond repeated modifications within unusual core families.
transferable_gaps.generator_implication: Broaden distinct stable core and linker arrangements that preserve useful functionality, beyond peripheral substitutions and alternate ring closures. Treat functional-group electronic context and spatial placement as chemical properties, with usefulness determined by observed feedback rather than a prescribed objective-specific scaffold.

method_name: Tabu search: de novo graph walks with expiring structural prohibitions
method_thesis: The anchor is the basic tabu-search procedure in Section 2 of [Glover, Tabu Search—Part I](https://leeds-faculty.colorado.edu/glover/TS%20-%20Part%20I-ORSA-aw.pdf), fixed before locating this external source. It chooses the best available admissible move, including a worsening move, while temporarily prohibiting reversals through short-term attribute memory. My molecular adaptation starts from the best supplied observation and maintains one current molecular graph, its true score, an independent best-observed archive, and expiring structural restrictions. At each feedback step, stochastically generate a new neighborhood through atom and bond edits, additions, deletions and chemically checked ring changes. Define move attributes from presence/absence changes of canonical local subgraphs around the edited region. After selecting a move, temporarily forbid a bounded record of its inverse attribute changes. These restrictions must apply to different canonical molecules sharing the affected local chemistry, so they can alter search beyond the protocol's mandatory whole-molecule duplicate rejection. Generate valid, canonical-unique, admissible neighbors until the announced batch is filled, then submit them directly without a learned score predictor. Only after real feedback choose the highest-scoring accepted neighbor as the next current graph, even when it scores below the current graph; retain the best score seen anywhere. Age restrictions by completed walk steps. If restrictions prevent sufficient fresh generation, release the oldest restrictions only as needed and record that release. This root uses the basic tabu form without an aspiration rule requiring unknown candidate scores. Preparation needs no learned model or corpus molecule store. Each objective restarts the same task-agnostic procedure with clean labeled and tabu state, and every proposed structure is generated online from the evolving current graph. The hypothesis is that an aggressive observed-neighbor choice combined with temporary structural reversal restrictions can move through useful intermediate structures and reach higher scoring molecular regions within the supplied feedback schedule. Activation requires restrictions to veto otherwise valid novel structural moves and thereby influence later current states. That diagnostic is insufficient by itself: success is the mean of the five independent final Top-1 scores. Overbroad attributes may suppress productive chemistry, while overly specific attributes may never affect novel proposals; the root must expose both possibilities.

applicability_conditions: The registered class is a physical bond with F, Cl, Br or I at one endpoint and a non-carbon heavy atom at the other, independent of charge, isotope, ring status or bond order. H-X and C-X bonds are outside it; a halogen-halogen bond is one counted bond. These endpoint definitions are the mechanism, not a complete chemical-alert system.

The count is source-relative. Existing counted bonds can persist or be replaced at equal total count, and removing one is allowed. All supplied initial current graphs happen to have zero counts, permitting a stronger zero-count trajectory prediction here without editing initialization.

Some direct N/O/S-halogen molecules have uses as reactive reagents, and the Parent obtains real score gains from some counted attachments. The experiment tests avoiding this persistent class in the campaign's proposed molecules, not a claim that every such chemical graph is impossible or always scores badly.

Carbon-halogen eligibility and the complete inherited alphabet remain intact. Actual retention of that channel is measured from evaluated chemistry, while unrelated sulfur valence, ring geometry, N-O/N-N bonds and stereochemistry remain outside the gate's claim.

The earlier sulfur-envelope cluster and corpus-supported environment cluster use different predicates and evidence. This fixed bond-count criterion has no existing curated attempt; their filtering implementations are not inherited, widened or combined with it.

molecular_assessment.headline: Tightly sized ring-rich molecules retain unusual sulfur centres, dense bridges and undefined stereochemistry
molecular_assessment.overall_character: The complete panel contains 900 evaluated molecules per task across three seeds, including 870 optimizer proposals each. All 4,350 optimizer proposals parse with RDKit. Every proposal contains a ring-closure digit, and digest aromatic-token rates range from 0.8667 to 1.0; rings are abundant. Proposal heavy-atom ranges are tightly concentrated at 21-29, 30-48, 29-43, 28-45 and 26-34 in fixed task order, with no proposal above 50 heavy atoms. Nevertheless, these are not uniformly simple molecules: median ring counts are three, four, four, five and six, and the last task reaches 17 perceived rings within its limited atom range. Recognizable ketones, thioesters, lactams, ethers, phenols and amines coexist with unusual sulfur coordination, highly fused or bridged graphs and small unsaturated rings. Proposals with explicit-H sulfur atoms bonded to at least two heavy atoms number 50, 138, 747, 192 and 554. These [SH] sites should not be read as ordinary terminal thiols. Direct N-halogen and O-halogen bonds are absent from current proposals, whereas they occurred in the parent, but unusual sulfur and ring chemistry remains pervasive. All proposals have zero charged-string markers; neutrality does not establish ordinary valence chemistry or stable solution species. Per-task nonchiral Murcko scaffold counts are 430, 418, 452, 442 and 521, while leaders remain concentrated in a few related families. No proposal assigns a stereocentre; 624, 396, 870, 668 and 780 contain unassigned centres. I read the dominant sulfur-rich high-score families as implausible practical synthetic targets without substantial chemical validation, while some ketone, thioester and lactam alternatives are more recognizable. The assessment concerns chemical appearance, not demonstrated synthesis or activity.

The next family is more recognizable: substituted indene-like ketones or heteroaryl thioesters, often with amino, alkoxy or bromoethyl groups. Several carry an O/N/S-substituted carbon connected to a bromomethyl group, a chemically different motif from a simple ether. Parent leaders included N-halogenated amide or sulfur-containing fused frameworks. Current direct N-halogen proposals fall from 172 to zero, but sulfur and ring-bond alterations persist. Full proposals have median 25 heavy atoms and three rings.

Bromomethyl or bromoethyl arms and O/N/S-substituted carbons introduce potential reactivity and stability questions.
Sulfur double-bond and coordination changes must be assessed in context; ordinary thioesters should not be equated with unusual cyclic sulfur centres.

The leading three-membered N-ring and heteroatom-rich side-chain structures lack established geometry or synthetic access, and 624 proposals have unassigned centres.
